title: Bagging, Blending & Stacking
interviewAnswer: Bagging, voting, blending and stacking combine models for different reasons. Bagging averages resampled versions of an unstable learner to reduce variance. Voting or averaging combines independently trained model outputs using fixed or learned weights. Stacking trains a meta-model on out-of-fold base predictions so it can learn where models complement one another; using in-sample base predictions leaks fit quality and usually overweights flexible learners. Blending uses a dedicated holdout for meta-training and sacrifices data. For classification I align class order and use probabilities or decision scores consistently, with calibration when needed. I require every base and meta feature to be available at the same prediction cutoff, use grouped or temporal folds, compare against the best single model and simple average, and ship fallbacks for partial model failure.
keyPoints: Ensembling helps when component errors are usefully diverse, not merely when model names differ.
Stacking meta-features must be out-of-sample with respect to each base model.
Fold design must preserve time, groups and preprocessing boundaries for the entire two-level pipeline.
Probability scales and class-column order must be compatible before averaging or meta-learning.
A production ensemble needs dependency, latency, fallback and version-skew contracts.
why: Model combination can improve robustness and accuracy, but it can also package leakage, correlated errors and operational fragility behind one score. Stacking is especially instructive because its training data are predictions created by another training procedure. Correctness therefore depends on provenance at two levels: every meta-feature must be generated by a base estimator that did not train on that row, and all preprocessing must obey the same boundary. The method teaches when diversity matters, why a simple average is a demanding baseline, how probability calibration affects blending, and why a meta-model can overfit a small out-of-fold table. At deployment, the ensemble is a dependency graph with multiple artifacts, feature transforms, deadlines and failure modes. Learning these details turns 'combine several models' into a reproducible system design rather than an accidental leaderboard trick.
intuition: Several forecasters make different mistakes. A fixed average assumes each deserves the same voice. A weighted vote gives trusted forecasters more influence everywhere. Stacking hires an editor who learns patterns such as 'trust the tree on nonlinear segment A but the linear model on sparse segment B.' The editor must review predictions made on cases the forecasters had not already memorized. If it sees their training predictions, an overfit forecaster looks perfect and wins too much weight. Out-of-fold predictions simulate honest auditions, after which base models can be refit on all training data for service.
deepDive: Ensembling is error-correlation engineering under a strict data-lineage contract. Bagging, fixed aggregation and stacking solve different problems. Stacking constructs a second supervised dataset from honest base predictions, then refits deployable base models. Its statistical benefit must exceed meta-overfit and its operational benefit must exceed the latency and reliability cost of a multi-artifact graph.
workedExample: Two unbiased regressors each have error variance 4 and error correlation 0.75. Their equal average has variance (1/4)(4+4+2*0.75*4)=3.5, only a small gain over 4. If correlation were zero, variance would be 2. A slightly weaker but complementary model can therefore add more ensemble value than another copy of the strongest model.

commonMistakes.misconception: Any collection of diverse algorithms will improve performance.
commonMistakes.correction: What matters is useful error diversity under deployment, not different brand names. Measure residual correlation and honest incremental value.

commonMistakes.misconception: Train the meta-model on predictions from bases fitted to all training rows.
commonMistakes.correction: Those are in-sample and leak fit quality. Use out-of-fold or dedicated holdout predictions.

commonMistakes.misconception: Soft voting can average any numeric score.
commonMistakes.correction: Class order, label meaning and scale must align; logits, margins and probabilities have different semantics.

commonMistakes.misconception: A stack's latency is just the average base latency.
commonMistakes.correction: Online fan-out, the slowest dependency, serialization and meta inference determine tail latency and reliability.

followUps.question: Why refit base models after creating OOF features?
followUps.answer: OOF models train on only part of the data. The deployment bases are refit on all training data, while the meta-model retains the honest relationship learned from OOF predictions.

followUps.question: Blending versus stacking?
followUps.answer: Blending uses one held-out meta-training set and is simpler but data-inefficient; stacking uses folds to create out-of-fold predictions for every row.

followUps.question: Should raw features pass through to the meta-model?
followUps.answer: Only when conditional trust is needed and nested validation supports it; passthrough increases capacity, leakage surface and serving dependencies.

production: Version every base pipeline, its training cutoff and output schema, the fold manifest that created meta-features, class order, target transformation, meta-model, calibration, threshold and compatible ensemble manifest. Execute independent bases in parallel within explicit deadlines and record per-component latency and artifact IDs. Train and test a declared response to missing or late bases; never inject an unseen sentinel. Monitor each base output, disagreement and correlation, meta input distribution, final score, calibration, delayed loss, fallback rate and version skew. Protect prediction traces that expose sensitive component behavior. Canary the complete compatible bundle and compare against the best-single fallback. Roll back atomically to the previous base-plus-meta manifest when schema, latency, calibration or decision outcomes fail.
math: For regression predictions f_m(x), a weighted ensemble is f(x)=Σ_m a_m f_m(x), often with a_m≥0 and Σ_m a_m=1. Its error variance is a^TΣ_e a, so covariance matters. In K-fold stacking, z_im=f_m^(-fold(i))(x_i) is generated by a model excluding i's fold; meta-learner g fits y_i on z_i (and optionally approved original features). At deployment, refit each f_m on all training data and predict g(f_1(x),...,f_M(x)). Classification columns must share class order and transformation.

lab.goal: Construct leakage-free out-of-fold regression meta-features, fit a stack and verify fold coverage and baseline improvement.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
rng=np.random.default_rng(4); X=rng.uniform(-2,2,(120,2)); y=1.5*X[:,0]+X[:,1]**2+rng.normal(0,.15,120)
kf=KFold(5,shuffle=True,random_state=5); oof=np.zeros((len(X),2)); seen=np.zeros(len(X),int)
for train,val in kf.split(X):
    models=[LinearRegression(),DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3,random_state=0)]
    for j,m in enumerate(models): oof[val,j]=m.fit(X[train],y[train]).predict(X[val])
    seen[val]+=1
meta=LinearRegression().fit(oof,y)
base_full=[LinearRegression().fit(X,y),DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3,random_state=0).fit(X,y)]
stack_train=meta.predict(oof)
lab.verifyIt:
assert np.array_equal(seen,np.ones(len(X),int))
assert np.isfinite(oof).all()

description: Ensembling combines predictors through resampling, fixed aggregation or learned meta-models. This chapter distinguishes bagging, hard and soft voting, weighted averaging, blending and stacking, then derives why error covariance determines ensemble gain. It develops the complete out-of-fold stacking algorithm, including fold-local preprocessing, class-column alignment, optional passthrough features, meta-regularization and final base-model refitting. Worked examples calculate the variance of correlated predictors and expose leakage from in-sample meta-features. The lab builds regression stacking with explicit out-of-fold predictions, compares it with scikit-learn and verifies one-time fold coverage, finite meta-features and performance against a mean baseline. Production guidance treats the ensemble as a dependency graph: artifact lineage, parallel execution, deadlines, partial failures, version skew, feature cutoffs, monitoring, canaries and rollback are explicit. The standard of evidence is strict: a stack should beat the best component and a simple average on honest data by enough to justify its added complexity. You will also learn how class-column ordering and score calibration affect aggregation, why outer evaluation must wrap the entire stack construction, and how an atomic manifest prevents incompatible base and meta-model versions.
learningObjectives: Explain when bagging, voting, averaging, blending and stacking can reduce error.
Construct leakage-free out-of-fold meta-features under grouped or temporal folds.
Align probability scales, class order and final refitting between training and inference.
Design an ensemble serving graph with resource budgets and partial-failure fallbacks.

deepSections.title: Different ensembles solve different error problems
deepSections.body: Bagging retrains a base algorithm on resampled data and averages predictions, primarily targeting estimator variance. Random forests add feature randomness. Hard voting counts labels and discards confidence; soft voting averages probabilities and assumes their scales are comparable. Weighted averaging can constrain weights to a simplex for stability or learn unconstrained coefficients with regularization. Blending reserves a holdout to train the combiner, creating honest meta-features but reducing data for base fitting. Stacking uses folds so every training row receives out-of-fold base predictions. Boosting is also an ensemble but learns members sequentially against current error rather than training a separate meta-model. Choose the mechanism from an error hypothesis. Ten nearly identical gradient-boosting seeds may add little because their errors are highly correlated; a weaker model can add value if it is right on different cases.

deepSections.title: Out-of-fold predictions are a new training dataset
deepSections.body: Partition the training units into folds using the same group or time constraints as deployment. For each fold, fit every base pipeline on the other folds and predict the held-out fold. Store those predictions in their original row positions; each row must be predicted exactly once by a model that excluded it. Fit the meta-learner on this complete matrix. Preprocessing, feature selection, calibration and base hyperparameter tuning must occur inside the appropriate training boundary. If base hyperparameters were selected on all folds, nested structure may be required for an unbiased performance estimate. In-sample predictions are invalid because flexible bases appear unrealistically accurate. After meta-training, refit each chosen base pipeline on all available training data. Deployment feeds these full-fit predictions to the frozen meta-model, assuming their distribution is compatible with the out-of-fold predictions used during meta-training.

deepSections.title: Keep the meta problem small and well conditioned
deepSections.body: The out-of-fold table has n rows but may contain strongly correlated columns. A flexible meta-model can overfit it, especially after many candidate bases, transformations and feature passthroughs were tried. Start with a regularized linear or logistic combiner and compare with equal averaging and the best component. Nonnegative simplex weights improve interpretability and prevent extreme cancellation, though they may limit useful corrections. For multiclass classification, each base may contribute K probability or score columns with a fixed class order; dropping one redundant probability column can improve conditioning. Calibrate bases before soft voting only using honest data, or allow a meta-model to learn scale differences while evaluating final calibration separately. Passthrough of raw features lets the meta-model learn conditional trust but increases leakage and complexity risk. Report ablations and stability of weights across folds.

deepSections.title: Prove complementarity and incremental value
deepSections.body: Use an outer grouped or temporal test around the entire stack-building procedure. Measure the task metric, uncertainty across splits, calibration and thresholded decision utility. Compare every base, the best base selected without test leakage, equal averaging and the stack. Inspect residual correlations and slice performance to understand complementarity. A small average gain with high variance may not survive. Test missing-base scenarios and late predictions. Avoid selecting dozens of bases on one test set; that turns ensemble composition into test overfitting. For classification, align positive labels and class columns, and distinguish averaging logits from probabilities. For regression, check units and transformations such as log targets before combination. A model that only improves rare slices may still be valuable if those slices are operationally important, but that value should be explicitly measured rather than hidden in aggregate score.

deepSections.title: Serve a versioned prediction graph
deepSections.body: An online stack may call multiple models in parallel, concatenate outputs and invoke a meta-model. Define a common feature cutoff, deadline and schema. Record base and meta artifact IDs in every prediction trace. A late or failed base cannot silently become zero unless the meta-model was trained for that sentinel. Options include a reduced fallback meta-model, cached safe prediction, best-single-model route or explicit unavailability. Budget CPU, memory and network fan-out; the slowest dependency often controls tail latency. Monitor each base distribution, pairwise disagreement, meta weights or contributions, final score, calibration, delayed error, fallback rate and version skew. Canary the complete graph, not one component in isolation. Rollback must restore a compatible set of base models and meta-model because mixing generations can shift meta-feature distributions.

If correlation were zero, variance would be 2. A slightly weaker but complementary model can therefore add more ensemble value than another copy of the strongest model.

workedExamples.title: In-sample stacking leaks base flexibility
workedExamples.body: A deep tree predicts its training labels perfectly while logistic regression reaches 80 percent. A meta-model trained on those same predictions assigns nearly all weight to the tree. On new users, the tree falls to 65 percent. Out-of-fold tree predictions would have exposed that behavior and allowed the combiner to learn from honest relative performance.

exercises.prompt: Why is an equal average an important baseline?
exercises.solution: It gains diversity without fitting a meta-model. A stack that cannot reliably beat it may not justify extra statistical and operational complexity.

exercises.prompt: How do grouped folds change stacking?
exercises.solution: Every OOF base model must exclude the entire group of each validation row, preventing entity leakage into meta-features.

exercises.prompt: A base model times out. Can its probability be replaced by zero?
exercises.solution: Only if the meta-model was explicitly trained and validated with that missingness encoding. Otherwise route to a compatible fallback.
